All right, we got them down there documented for posterity. Turn her off.
How old are those? How old are those?
About those at Easter Side.

That's about a week before that. A week and a half old was that. We're ready to start any time you are. You can get your full name first. Okay. We're going to ask you a few questions. What is your name, Ernie?
Ernie Joseph Cagnoletti.
Just how do you pronounce it? Do you pronounce that G in there? We were just talking, you know, some Italian names you don't pronounce for G. I'm wondering...
Is it Cagnoletti or Cagnoletti?
Cagnoletti. Cagnoletti.
I'll mention that this is Bill Russell interviewing. Your home, what's the address?
3650 in Buchanan.
And also Ralph Collins and Harold A. John are present to help with the interview. Can you tell us just when you were born and just where, what part of this city, if it was right here in town?
I was born April 2nd, 1911 in Madisonville, Louisiana. On the other side of Punchetran Lake.

Can you tell us about your parents? Really just ask a few questions now and then. This doesn't have to be in any special order. We can jump back and forth in your life. It doesn't matter if it's all right straight into what you live. Can you tell us about your parents? Did they play any instrument?
Well, no, they didn't actually play an instrument, but they was musically inclined. How did you like to play that? My elder brother, he was a musician. He was a drummer.
Is he living?

No, he died in 1941. What was his name? Yeah, Cagnoletti. Cagnoletti. He played with Bung Johnson during World War I in Madisonville when they were launching ships. And that would give me my inspiration to play trumpet by here in Bung Johnson. That's the first trumpet player I've ever heard.
What did your brother play? He played drums.

What did you play? That started me playing music at the age of five. I started playing drums. In fact, he had two sets. And when he would leave Madison to go around Ibiza Spring, those places to play with Bung Johnson, he'd leave a set of drums at the Sons of Leobol in Madisonville where I think in those days it was showing silent pictures. He had a piano player while the pianola would play during the pitch and when the pitch was over, she would play the piano. Her name was Leona Bayham. She'd play the piano and I'd play the drums for her. And I was about five years old at that time.
And you remember anything about the band that Bung was in? Who was the band?

Oh yes. Who else? Matter of fact, I have a sister-in-law that his wife, my brother's wife has the picture of the band, but I've been trying to get it for him. And I'm Trill's time to get it for him. She lives on Orleans Street. And I hope someday she will let me have it. And in that band, the leader of the band was Joe Fritz, the daddy, he played bass. And one of the brothers was Earl Fritz, he played the trombone. And Isidore Fritz was a piano player, also was the teacher of George Lewis.
Yeah, George has told us about him a little bit.
And Leon Pyron was the guitar player. And my brother played drums and Bung Johnson was the trumpet player.
Earl Foster told us a little bit about that band, he mentioned you too.

Yeah, well he lived in Maddenville, you see. And every time that Janker would launch a ship during World War I, 1917 in the Shifunksu River, they would come and play for the luncheon of the ship. And when they'd come and do that, well they'd always stay home, see. But during the time they were home they'd rehearsal and they'd play joys from, leave from my house and play right around those little country towns like that. And he would come back there. And in 1919, my brother came here to live and I came with him.
Did you know Andy Anderson over that part of the country too?
Andrew Anderson, yeah he lived in Maddenville too, Earl Foster, he's from Maddenville. A cousin I believe was there. Yeah, first cousin Earl Foster.
He told us he heard Bung too when he was a kid.
Yeah, he saw Bung too.
And you know Tommy Ladner over there, was that before your time?
No, I didn't know Tommy Ladner.
He left pretty young.
No, I didn't know Tommy.
Well we're thinking of other people over there, did you ever...

I'll tell you who I did see over there, there was a man by the name of Professor Divergis. He was something like pinch back at that time, would go around teaching youngsters that didn't quite have enough means to go to school. And they had another group of fellas in Madisonville, it was Joe Clark who played the violin, his daddy played the bass, and Joe, let's see what this guy's name, he was a high school, he played trombone. And then Paul Santon was a guitar player, well he taught them, there was about six of them.
The Voidners taught mostly scholars for nothing.
That's right, that's what he did.
Was that Charlie Divergis, who's named Charlie? Yeah.
I have to know, Jerry's a professor and never studied from him when he was in jail.

He's from here, he's from New Orleans, but he would come to Madisonville and go to Manderville, it'd be the spring at Covington, to all the schools, and donate most of each time to teach music to young students. My brother went to him too.
Well when you started on drums, did you say you had your own set, they had a couple sets in the band?
No, my brother had two sets and he would leave a set and he would go out with the other.
Did you ever know Dan Moody?

Oh yes, Dan Moody from Madisonville, he played trombone and bass. Matter of fact he just died about a year or two years ago. Can you tell us anything about him? Not in particular, I didn't play with Dan until 1952, let me see, it was the year that President Roosevelt died. I happened to be in the beauty spring, he'd come here to get me to play a job with him, and we played over there. You don't know what? And he had been playing with different fellas we'd make up groups from out of Punchitula and Covington, he had a piano player live in company, he'd go around and pick them up and they would play at this Duvors pavilion in Manderville. See, that's where this boat used to land from at the Millenbury, they'd catch these boats and they had that excursion every and Sunday with the Susquehanna. Little Susquehanna. And they would land at the Duvors place, well that place stood up till the last part of 1953 or something like that. Yeah. And he had a regular job there off and on and he would play in Buggaloosa, but he never kept in a regular group. He would go around and pick up different fellas.
He used to come here and get Sheep to go to the Covington Fair with him.
Yeah, Sheep used to play. You went over with Sheep and her body?
Yeah, out in Franklin. She used to go out there in Franklin and play with him on those fairs, Covington too. He played quite a few jobs there with him.
Can you tell us about your first drums when you started to take it up? Did you have any lessons? Did your brother help you with it or did you just pick it up?
No, I just actually picked it up. It was in me and I just picked it up.
About how much older was your brother than you?
Oh, he's the oldest one in the family. Right now he would be about 63. No, he would be about 68 right now.
How much older than you is that then?
He's 50 that day. I made 50 Sunday.
Oh, you're dead? Yeah. 18 years older than you. 18 years older than that.
Yeah, because when he was playing with Bung Johnson then he was in short pants. Of course you couldn't tell it because he's sitting behind the bass drum. Yeah. And you have a picture of that band?
My sister don't have it.
I've been trying to get it for me. I'd like to see that.
We could make a copy of it.
Yeah, that's what I'd do. I'd like to put a camera in front of it. Joe Mraz even tried to get it for me, you know. I'm still going to try to get it.
You think she'd let him take a picture of it?
We could go to her home and take it if she wouldn't mind. We don't like to disturb everybody.
I'm going to try to get it for you.
We could make a new negative and you could get the prints ever too.
So you could have a copy of it. She's the first think I wouldn't bring it back. Yeah.
That might be the best thing if we just go to her home and take a strong light. A couple of these reading lamps like that, you know. Turn on one each side and snap it. Just take a photograph of it.
Leave it right there.
Take it through a free time and get a good one.
This project on Orleans Street and I have to find it just what important she lives in.

We'll see you sometime. I'm going to try to get it for you. Well, we'd be glad to go there. It wouldn't take but a few minutes to go to her home and do it. She wouldn't have to worry about losing it because I don't blame her for not running alone and things like that to people she doesn't know.
Did you continue playing drum until you started playing trumpet or? Oh no.
I left Madisonville in 1919. I came over here and lived with my brother. And at that time, he came here and joined the band with Albert Glennie and...
Albert Duconge played trumpet.

And this guy that used to call him Nutzi. I believe his name was Alonzo who was playing clarinet. And Ambrose on trombone. I forget who was playing the banjo. Well that's the band he was with then. Was there any special name to that band? No, they didn't have a special name to that band or? No, they didn't have a special name to that particular band at that time. And I was living with him then. And occasionally I would go around when he would go and play, he would take me with him.
See?

And later on around 1924, 25 like that, he would take me out on jobs and he would leave me sit down and sit down and play. And I played myself with George Lewis and D.D. and Billy on drums. Did you tell us yet when you started trumpet? You played drums a long time then. Well just off and on, just filling in. You were 17. 1927 I started playing trumpet in 1927. He was my teacher there. He was my teacher there. He was stuff with with George Lewis and Dee Dee and Billy on drums. Did you tell us yet when you started trumpet? I started playing trumpet 1927. You were playing drums a long time then. Just filling in. 1927 I started on trumpet on all my twi. He was my teacher. He taught me just about, I think it was about five years after he turned Albert Snaya. Albert Snaya was one of his last students he had before I went to him. Matter of fact, I wanted to go on Manuel Perez, that's who his brother was on. But he had stopped teaching at the time so I went on Alma Twi. He was a very good teacher.
How long did you stay with him?

Well I stayed with Alma Twi for about two years. You started right at the beginning? And then he died. Have you been blowing on the horn at all? No, right from the beginning. But it was about, I took about sixteen lessons before he'd ever let me touch the horn. Just reading music? Just reading music and then after I did that then he would let his daughter go in the rum and make chords on the piano and make me distinguish between the minors and the majors. Oh yeah. And then he, when he did get the horn, he took it all apart and made me name the parts of the horn and told me how to assemble it together. Then he started me to play.
Did you have any book for that self edge or whatever they call it? For that book? The reading and all that. Did he make you sing those things?
Oh yeah, yeah, yeah. Oh yeah. I had to hum the minor chords and the major chords as she would call me and distinctly tell him which was which.
Did you have any book for that or did he write it out?

No, he didn't have no book. It actually was a year training from the other room. What she was doing I'm supposed to detect me, tell him whether it was a minor or a major. He would have me guessing whether she was playing in sharps or flats. You see, about a year training from that time. But I hadn't even touched the horn as yet. And he started me on the horn and after I got up away, he told me that, Don't go play with nobody. Better than a year, two years before he would let me play with anybody. And then when I did go out, I started playing with small groups, different fellas.

Oh, interrupted. About those lessons, I was interested since Mr. Matriya is gone. We did talk to his widow and daughter. Yeah. And they told us quite a bit about him. But I wondered in his teaching, did he use a certain method? What method do you remember?
Well, I'll tell you one thing he was. Yes, he was very determined in teaching here. And he had very much patience. He would give you a lesson and...
Remember any method book that he used?

Well, yeah, he bought, you know, the first book he bought me was a French Pocharon book. I don't know him. No, he got that, true of his, Vorice, which he used to play first trumpet at the Offsen Theatre, I believe his brother would say that. Yeah, true of his brother. Well, see, they were very good friends. He got the book for him. And after I finished that book, then he got me one of these Auburn Methods. Oh, yeah. I remember that. That's the book he brought me through, the Auburn Method. And then when I went out and started playing... Well, to get on...
I appreciate you telling me that. I wasn't right to interrupt you. Yeah. I wanted to find out more about the lessons. How often did you go there?
Well, twice a week. Twice a week? Twice a week, yeah. And then...
About how long did they last?
An hour. One hour. And everybody charged for the lessons? Yeah, fifty cents a lesson.
That's all.

Fifty cents a lesson. And after my fourteenth lesson, he promised me that every lesson that I would bring back to him, and if I knew it, I wouldn't have to pay him. For his. That's right. And he would always give my lesson, and from then on I ain't given fifty cents yet. I was fighting him. He was really tickled to death about it.
No teacher would do that nowadays.
Matter of fact it was hard to get 50 cents too at that time. That meant a good deal.
Did he teach you anything about time, padding your foot or anything?

Oh yeah, I mean, that French Pochelon method, I've never seen nobody here with one like that. Of course, they have those diagrams now, made in a circle with your arrows pointing each way to show you. And with the dialect in the center, with the time on it, see? And you'll have in your mind an imaginary needle to keep your time for you. But your foot had to act as the needle, see? That's the get you used to playing without paying attention to your foot. And if your foot be trying to it, that you could keep that time, even if you got, say, an eight-bar layout or something, and you could go out on and hold a conversation with somebody, and you can tell from your foot, just wanting to come back in with it. Of course, you can do it easily on arrangements without doing that. But if you plan stocks, you actually got to come.
Yeah. Did he sort of, your foot down on the first beat?
Down on the first beat and up on the second.
Up on the second, down on the third, and up on the fourth. On the fourth, that's right. And for three, four times?
Well, it would be like this. Down, out, and up. That would be the two and up. That would be the two. Down and up.
Slide it out and then out.

Now, some of the teachers... But that's the Manetta still teaches. That's the same system? That's his system, too. Now, some of the others, they'll give you one down, one out, one in, and one up on your comma time, four.
That's the way a Shalini taught you. One, two, three, four.

But Manetta... No, it didn't. It was one down and one up. In other words, you made two beats. Now, four concerts started making one out, two, three, four. It was one, two, three, four. You see? You count two down and two up.

That was your four. I've heard that Arnaud Mottwey was famous for his non-pressure playing. He could walk up to a trumpet like hanging on a string and lower things like that. You could do that. Did he ever stress that in his lessons? That was not for you, not the first measure? Did he do anything special to teach you that?

Well, no. He didn't actually stress to me about the non-pressure system of playing. Even when he started me on double-tonging and triple-tonging, he wanted me to use... By me being so young, he wanted me to build the muscles up in my lips. See, that was the general idea. The non-pressure system, you don't use much muscles, you see. And he wanted me to build the muscles up in my lips. So he wanted me to play the natural way. Which he could play both ways, you understand? Yeah. But he mostly used the non-pressure system like he was playing the jitney house on the music box on Canal and Crudlin at that time.
Yeah, I heard that.

And after playing them jitneys there for maybe six, seven hours, they'd play all night in the air for the day. When he'd get tired, he'd start playing in the non-pressure system and just like starting all over, see. His lips wouldn't get tired.
Did he say anything about playing with wet lips or dry lips or anything like that?

No, he was more in favor of playing with your lips wet, see. That moist lips keep from cracking. You see, dry lips, what actually happens, I could say it in a lot of time, your throat gets dry too. And your mouthpiece, nine out of ten, will stick to your lip. And if you move it, well, you slip off your armature, you see. Where they're wet, they're not going to slip off your armature. All you would have to leave your lips stay wet and just wipe their mouthpiece off and put it right back, see. And it'll fall right back in place.
Do most trumpet players play with their lips wet? I never think about that, Arden. I never played drumming to start with.
I think the majority of them do. I mean, it looks like it comes natural to them. It just comes natural to them.
So they got some of them all in there. What about the mouthpiece? Did he say anything about any special kind of mouthpiece?
Well, no, he didn't. He let me choose whatever he figured would fit my armature better, you know. He was very particular of me trying to play in the center of my mouth.
Oh, right in the center?

In the center. If I could build a muscle up in the center, you see, that would keep too much air pressure from coming out on each side. See, if you're too much to one side, this side gets weak. You're not strengthening this side because you're not planting in the middle. See, eventually air going to come out of here and you're going to puff out on this side or you're going to puff out. But direct in the center, you breathe down in your stomach. You don't breathe from the side of your mouth.
Did you have a wide cushioned rim mouthpiece or a narrow mouthpiece? Do you remember?
No, my mouthpiece was always cushioned rim. I started with it. My first trumpet was a Kahn 22B. It was a Silver Kahn 22B Kahn at that time.
Was it a Kahn-ed or a trumpet?
No, a trumpet. A trumpet, yeah. 1927.
You had a Kahn-ed piece with it?
A Kahn-ed piece with it. Speaking of the position on the lips, you usually hold it more on the upper lip or the lower lip?

No, more on the lower lip. More on the lower lip. He didn't teach me that, but he asked me to try to use that method because that's what it's actually. In Auburn, that's from old man Auburn, that's his method, and it seems to be most of the trumpet players that played with Sousa used that method. Most of all those have road methods, and they have that same system.
There's Herbert Clark.
I see Howard James got that same system. Listen, you see the idea is this. You get a better support because the thicker part of it, that's more strength there, you see.
In the lower lip.

Yeah, and then your lip support it more, you see. Well, if you put your strength up here, you see, because you're going to push more with the bottom lip than you would the top. So you get most of your support down here. Then, even if you're hitting high notes, it's more easy for you to sub down from your lip and hit the lower lip than if you were up here. You see, you didn't get very much grip on the top.
Did he say anything about your teeth? Did he think that your teeth were important?

Well, yeah, let you take good care of your teeth, you see. And one thing he knows is, you know, if they're not projecting out in a way like that, that kind of, you know, way hurts you. If you're in a way that projecting teeth, they couldn't make no good trumpet players.

I guess most trumpet players think of their teeth as a friend of mine, a young white trumpet player, Jerry Blumberg, staying here in town for about a week. I offered him some candy on Easter, some Easter eggs. He said, no, he's a trumpet player. He won't eat any candy. He thinks about his teeth. He's crazy. Yeah. Played to eat candy.
It's a good thing to think about it, right?
It might affect, yeah, I guess. Did you ever know any trumpet players much with the false teeth that played? I know Bunk Johnson finally played with false teeth.
Well, Bunk Johnson had false teeth. Gilbert Young has false teeth.
Oh, is that right?

Yeah. And he plays good. He'd take them out and play. He'd take them out and play without a team. He'd have none precious system about this world. He'd take them out. He'd have false teeth. And old man Lewis the man had quite a few false teeth. You know Gilbert Youngkin though?

When you had, before you got them false teeth, Gilbert Youngkin playing the side, either side or the middle. He had all these games. He'd get tired. He'd play. You ever get tired there, he'd play. I'm with you all over his mouth. Yeah, I was seeing him get his lip all bust up and he said, well, who's stopping him from playing?

He said, I've got more lip. He was another one of those jitney men. You know, he'd been there. He was on the jitney a long time with Earl Foster too. Right over there on the canal at the Alamo. Yeah, that was before Alvin Alcorn went in there. He went and got young this day.

So far, this sounds like a trumpet lesson. There's one more question I have to ask before we move on to your life again. Did Mr. Matoy ever say anything about breathing, anything special, exercises on breathing or anything that he gave you?

Well, yeah, see, in fact, he taught me from the whole note of breathing at the end of each bar, if you can, that's where you take your breath. Unless you have a break in between the bar where you can take a breath and you're going to have a tie over to the next bar to keep you from turning that tie loose where you'll catch your breath right in between there.
I was thinking in particular like that.

And you can't detect when you're trying to lose because it's done so quick. It's just like automatic grace note in between it that you can't tell if it's, you're doing it accidental or if it's ripped.
I was thinking, did he have any exercises for using your diaphragm rather than just your upper lungs or anything of that kind? Did he ever talk about those things?
You mean in breathing?
Yeah, in breathing, you think about using your stomach in order to throw in full breath

and feel? That's the way he played. That's one system. I don't know whether he did it under his own training or where he was taught, but that's a method he used. He always stood up to play. He meant a jitney dance. He never did sit down to play drunk as long as he'd been playing. Every job he was on, he stood up.

And you know what he used to do? I know him have a sandwich in his hand and play his chorus. When the siphon player would play, he'd bite his hand and chew it and then he still might have a mouth full and he'd play that horn. It's just like if you don't have, it's just nothing. Yeah. I seen him do it.
We were talking about one of our trombone friends the other day, he keeps a lot of tobacco. He used to play. Well, he'd play.
And Arthur would do it, never spit no food in his hand.

I know you've heard of it. Out on the lake shore there, he used to play several jobs with old man Dave Perkins. Oh yeah, it's a new band. Yeah, out on the lake. And I know he used to play a job with them and he would be standing up, just like to do
right.
He just wouldn't sit down.
Bung Johnson used to like to stand up, not all the time, but quite often he'd stand up, usually especially when he'd take a solo and it wasn't just to show off.

I didn't know whether it was habitual with him or if it was just a system he had. Probably could breathe easier. Even in teaching me. He'd sit me down by the music stand up, and he'd stand up. When he'd get his horn and he'd say, we're going to play a duet, he'd be standing up, making me sit down, he'd stand up all the day.
When you played duets, did you both play the melody or did he play the harmony with you? Well we would switch.
He would play the melody and he'd play the harmony and he'd fight the verse and I'd call it.
You were going to go on with your life there. Excuse the interruption, he's one of the great trumpet players. We never knew him before.

Yes he was, he was very great. And like I was telling you, I started playing trumpet around here and some of the small outfits. No name outfit. I played quite a few jobs with Burbank and several jobs. And several jobs with two trumpets. I played a job with Kid Rene with Wooden Joe, you were the one with Joe Nickles. Boy I knew Wooden Joe, yeah very well. And also with Bill N. D. D. And I played a job with Paul Dominguez, the violinist. I played several jobs right there, especially during the pression. They had these little Bill Pauls was having bands, mostly on the weekends like that. And I played several jobs with Steve Lewis, Johnny Sancia, and Simon Marrero, and Steve Lewis and myself. Mostly a string outfit. Because after I know Matoyi had died, I was going to Paul Dominguez to take a few lessons with him. That was the violin player.
He was the violin player.

But he helped you with your reading you know? Yeah, he was a good musician. So when they would get a job like that, he would always cut me. And then I played some job with Willis San Diego. Doing the, out on Decatur Street during that time. Right after I left Harold, because I worked with Harold a good while on, at the Popeye on Decatur Street. He had an impression. He had an outfit out there. And I saw several jobs with George Lewis and Richard McLean and a bunch.
You stayed with George Lewis a good while ago?

Yeah, I think with George for about four years playing a different place. And then I went with Chester's Otis. Little Chester's Otis. He played bass player. He had a group with me and Howard Mandorf and Alexis Russel. You might have heard him. He's a saxophone player.
He's working with Whitney Bank there, the messenger. The same place that the bass player lived on. Eddie Dawson. Eddie Dawson. Yeah, yeah. He stopped playing music.
Yeah, I think he's one of those Jehovah's Witnesses.
Yeah, he joined that.
Oh, maybe I did hear him.
And Homer Eugene was in that outfit too at that time, playing guitar. And another fellow, I don't know if he's right now, they call him Titi. He used to play drum with Chris Kelly one time.
What do you call him?

Titi. He was a show drummer, but he was at the Nighthawk, crossing the car, you understand? Yeah, by the Nighthawk, yeah. That's right. When Chris Kelly was at the Gypsy Tee Room, he was over there. Yeah, I think I did hear him.
He had that Tee Room. We used to go to the Nighthawk somewhere and leave the Gypsy Tee Room at night.
That's right. You know, come over there.

Well, I think I would, Mr. Foster, Earl Foster was the man we interviewed two weeks ago. Uh-huh. You mentioned you might happen to have a picture of Buddy Petit. You know of anybody that has if you don't have.
Well, I don't have, I actually have a picture of him. I have the picture of the band with oil on it that had no name in it. There was one with the…
In 1944, S-Quaddy.

Yes, we have that. Well, that's one. I wonder… The one that's, the guy that's doing the singing that you have no name in it, that's Earl Foster. Yeah, he told us that. Yeah, he told us that. Yeah, yeah, that's him with the cap on, with the microphone, that's what. Yeah, he told us that. That's Earl Foster.

That's good. He told us that and I never even thought of that there'd be anybody that we'd ever meet, you know. And all of a sudden he tells us that it's nice to have him. That's Earl Foster. Did you ever see any other pictures of Buddy Petit?
Well, no, of course I saw Buddy himself.
Yeah, I've seen you ever heard about pictures of Buddy Petit. I've never even saw Buddy at once. I've seen some more pictures of Buddy.

I'll actually tell you the truth. It seemed like those guys actually weren't taking many pictures of bands at that. They mostly were taking pictures of the brass bands like the Uricka, the Excelsa, and the…

the Ornwood band and all those those the kind of pictures that was taken and organized jazz band like Mario Perez and them and and and uh uh Piron you know what they were like the fire masseuse with the cap and all well they had pictures of them but the ordinary outside thing man like uh uh

do you remember him as yeah playing that way yeah buddy buddy was one he was wonderful uh trumpet player mostly making them diminish cars he was great at that matter of fact most anybody that know him right now and they'll tell you and most of all the musicians at this time they'll tell if he or he are either kidding right there if they would move north before
he hit here for Miller good time yeah
